51.quote_or_event: “Balwand says that Khivi, the Guru’s wife, is a noble woman, who gives soothing, leafy shade to all. She distributes the bounty of the Guru’s Langar; the kheer - the rice pudding and ghee, is like sweet ambrosia.”
51.explanation: The bards Satta and Balwand praise Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad, who ran the community kitchen, as a noble woman whose management of the household's food made it a shelter and blessing for everyone.
51.tie_back: She embodies Valluvar's ideal life-partner, whose household skill and good qualities turn the home's means into generosity for others.
51.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Pauri 3, Rai Balwand and Satta Doom (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
51._accuracy_note: Strong fit on a wife's excellence shown in running the household's provision for others, though nothing is said of living within her husband's means, which is the second half of the Kural.

52.quote_or_event: “O bride, decorate yourself, after you surrender and accept your Husband Lord. Otherwise, your Husband Lord will not come to your bed, and your ornaments will be useless.”
52.explanation: Using the image of the bride-soul, Guru Amar Das teaches that outward finery counts for nothing unless it comes with inner surrender and love; only then are the ornaments 'acceptable and approved'.
52.tie_back: Like the Kural's claim that a household's splendour is worthless without the wife's excellence, the verse says that outer adornment is useless without the inner quality that gives it meaning.
52.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
52._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the logic (outward splendour is empty without inner worth) matches, but the verse is about the soul-bride and God, a spiritual rather than domestic relationship, and the roles are reversed.

53.quote_or_event: “From woman, man is born; within woman, man is conceived; to woman he is engaged and married. Woman becomes his friend; through woman, the future generations come... So, why call her bad? From her, kings are born.”
53.explanation: In the Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak answers the low view of women common in his time by showing that every stage of a man's life, from birth to marriage to descendants, depends on woman.
53.tie_back: Like Valluvar's paired questions (with her, what does a man lack; without her, what does he have?), the Guru shows that a man's whole life rests on woman.
53.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
53._accuracy_note: Reasonable to strong fit on woman as indispensable to a man's life, though the Guru speaks of women in general, not of the wife's particular excellence (maanbu) that the Kural makes the deciding factor.

54.quote_or_event: “One whose tongue does not touch falsehood; whose mind is filled with love for the Blessed Vision of the Pure Lord, whose eyes do not gaze upon the beauty of others’ wives...”
54.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan describes the truly pure person: marital fidelity, not looking with desire at another's wife, sits beside truthfulness and love of God as a sign of inner steadiness.
54.tie_back: The Kural prizes karpu, firm inner fidelity, as the greatest treasure; Sikh teaching also values that firmness, but asks it of men as much as of women.
54.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 274, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 9, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
54._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shares the value of steadfast fidelity as an inner quality, but it addresses men and does not call a faithful wife a treasure, which is the Kural's actual claim.

55.quote_or_event: “Do not call them ’Satee’, who burn themselves along with their husbands’ corpses. O Nanak! They alone are known as ’Satee’, who die from the shock of separation.” … “They are also known as ‘Satee’, who abide in modesty and contentment. They serve their Lord, and rise in the early hours to contemplate Him.”
55.explanation: Guru Amar Das, who opposed the burning of widows, redefines the honoured title sati: the truly faithful woman is not the one who dies on the pyre but the one who lives with modesty and contentment and rises early to remember the Lord.
55.tie_back: Like the Kural's devoted wife who rises each day in reverence, the true sati rises early in devotion; but in Sikh teaching that devotion goes to God, not to the husband as a deity.
55.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 787, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Saloks Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
55._accuracy_note: Next-best and partly a contrast: Sikhism honours a wife's faithfulness and early-morning devotion but would not have her worship her husband in place of God, and it has no teaching that such a wife can command the rain.

56.quote_or_event: “What is that word, what is that virtue, and what is that magic mantra? What are those clothes, which I can wear to captivate my Husband Lord?” … “Humility is the word, forgiveness is the virtue, and sweet speech is the magic mantra. Wear these three robes, O sister, and you will captivate your Husband Lord.”
56.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are in the Sikh scripture, has the bride ask what will win her husband, and answers that it is not clothes or charms but humility, forgiveness and sweet speech.
56.tie_back: Like Valluvar, who defines a true wife by a set of steady inner virtues rather than by appearance, Farid lists the qualities that make the bride truly a bride.
56.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Saloks 126-127 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
56._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the form (a list of virtues that define the true wife) matches, but the Husband here is God and the love is spiritual, not marital, and the virtues differ from the Kural's self-guarding and care for the family name.

57.quote_or_event: “Paying a fine under pressure does not bring either merit or goodness. That alone is a good deed, O Nanak! Which is done by one’s own free will.”
57.explanation: Guru Angad teaches that goodness forced from outside has no moral worth; only what is done freely, from within, counts as a good deed.
57.tie_back: It shares the principle behind Valluvar's dismissal of confinement and guards: virtue that is only imposed from outside is no virtue, and only inner self-restraint truly protects.
57.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 787, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 2, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
57._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the verse states the general principle (coerced goodness is worthless) but says nothing about women, seclusion or guarding; Sikh tradition's opposition to purdah fits the theme but could not be verified verbatim here.

58.quote_or_event: “Myriads of Sitas are there, cool and calm in their majestic glory. Their beauty cannot be described.”
58.explanation: In describing the realm of grace (karam khand), the Japji pictures it filled with countless Sitas, the figure remembered in Indian tradition as the model of the faithful wife, dwelling there in serene glory.
58.tie_back: Like the Kural's faithful wives who win great glory in the world of the celestials, the Japji places innumerable Sita-like souls in majestic glory in the higher realm.
58.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, Pauri 37, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
58._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Sita's name links to wifely faithfulness, but in the Japji these are spiritual heroes filled with God, not wives rewarded for honouring husbands, and Sikhism teaches no special heaven earned by wifely devotion.

59.quote_or_event: “According to the actions the mortal commits, so is he proclaimed.”
59.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that each person's standing, what they are called and known as, comes from their own deeds.
59.tie_back: Kural 59 ties a man's public standing to his wife's care for the family name; Sikh teaching instead roots each person's reputation in their own actions.
59.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 730, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
59._accuracy_note: Next-best only and largely a contrast: no SGGS passage found makes a husband's honour depend on his wife's conduct, and Sikh teaching places responsibility for reputation on each individual.

60.quote_or_event: “In the first round of the marriage ceremony, the Lord sets out His Instructions for performing the daily duties of married life. Instead of the hymns of the Vedas to Brahma, embrace the righteous conduct of Dharma, and renounce sinful actions.”
60.explanation: This is the first of the four Laavan, the hymns sung while the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib at a Sikh wedding (Anand Karaj); marriage itself is presented as a blessed, God-given path of righteous conduct.
60.tie_back: Like the Kural, which calls the wife's excellence the true blessing (mangalam) of a home, the Sikh marriage hymn makes righteous married life itself the auspicious thing, in place of ritual.
60.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 773, Raag Soohee, Chhant (Laavan), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
60._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shares the sense of marriage as auspicious and dharmic, but does not single out the wife's excellence or call good children its ornament.
